# Overview

The `computeDrift` extension runs alongside the existing numeric_stats check
and analyzes how the distribution of `value_as_number` changes over time for
every (concept, unit) combination. The goal is to move data quality checks
beyond pass/fail thresholds toward automated pattern detection — identifying
when a data source starts to drift, whether the drift is a transient anomaly
or a persistent baseline shift, and quantifying the magnitude of change.

Drift is enabled by default via the `computeDrift = TRUE` argument on
`executeDqChecks()`. It reuses the same collected Andromeda frame that
numeric_stats already streams from the CDM, so **no additional warehouse
queries are issued** — the incremental cost is local R computation only.

To disable:

```r
executeDqChecks(..., computeDrift = FALSE)
```

# Methods

For each (concept, unit) group, values are bucketed by calendar month.
Months with fewer than 30 observations are marked `insufficient_data` and
excluded from drift computation (but retained in the output with NA metrics).

## Origin baseline

The origin baseline is the pooled distribution of values from the first
12 months meeting the sample-size floor. Ten quantile-based bin edges are
computed from origin values, extended with `-Inf` and `+Inf` sentinels so
future months whose values fall outside the origin range are still counted.

## Rolling regime baseline

Bayesian changepoint detection (`bcp::bcp`) runs on the bivariate series of
monthly mean and standard deviation. It returns a posterior probability at
each month that a regime change occurred, and months are segmented into
regimes at posterior > 0.5. For each regime, a pooled histogram over the
regime's months serves as the "current normal" baseline.

Because `bcp`'s convention is that `posterior.prob[i]` is the probability of
a change *between* month *i* and *i+1*, the `is_regime_start` flag is derived
from a one-position lag on the posterior series. The raw `bcp_posterior`
column preserves bcp's original semantics.

## Distributional metrics

Three complementary metrics are computed for every eligible month, once
against the origin baseline and once against the current regime baseline:

- **PSI (Population Stability Index)** — sum over bins of
  `(actual - expected) * ln(actual / expected)`. Natural-log convention.
  Bounded below by 0; identical distributions give 0. Small ε = 1e-6
  substituted for zero bins. Industry rules of thumb: PSI < 0.1 stable,
  0.1–0.25 moderate drift, > 0.25 significant drift.
- **Wasserstein-1 distance** — via `transport::wasserstein1d`, computed on
  raw values (not on binned histograms). Value is in the original units of
  the measurement, so a Wasserstein of 3.2 mg/dL is immediately
  interpretable.
- **Jensen-Shannon divergence** — via `philentropy::JSD` in log2 units, so
  the value is bounded in [0, 1]. This is the metric underlying
  Sáez et al.'s `EHRtemporalVariability` package, so JSD scores are
  directly comparable to the temporal maps that package produces.

## Anomaly detection

A month is flagged as `is_anomaly = TRUE` when its `psi_current`
(vs. its own regime's baseline) exceeds the PSI threshold *and* the month
is not itself a regime start. Regime starts are excluded because they
are already captured in the regime change list.

A transient one-month spike (e.g., an ETL error affecting a single month
that reverts the following month) typically appears as a very short
regime — often just 1 month long — rather than as an anomaly within a
larger regime. The `regime_length_months` column makes it trivial to
distinguish transient regimes from persistent baseline shifts.

## Trend and seasonality tests

Two auxiliary tests run per concept to feed pattern classification:

- **Mann-Kendall trend test** (`Kendall::MannKendall`) — non-parametric
  test for monotonic trend, run on both the monthly mean series (does
  central tendency drift smoothly?) and the monthly `psi_origin` series
  (is drift accumulating over time?). Returns Kendall's tau in [−1, 1]
  and a two-sided p-value. |tau| > 0.7 with p < 0.05 is treated as a
  strong monotonic signal.
- **Lag-12 autocorrelation** (`stats::acf`) — detects annual seasonality
  in the monthly mean series. Significant when the ACF at lag 12 exceeds
  2/√n (approximate 95% white-noise threshold).

## Bimodality test

`diptest::dip.test` runs on the origin baseline and on the current
regime's pooled values. A significance flip (unimodal → bimodal or vice
versa) is what triggers the `bimodal_change` pattern — a change in the
*shape* of the distribution, not just its location.

## Priority score

`priority_score = max(psi_origin, psi_current) × log10(1 + total_n_obs)`

A single sortable number combining drift magnitude with data volume. A
concept drifting badly but with only 100 total observations is less
urgent than one drifting moderately with 100,000 observations. Sorting
the drift summary by this score puts the most-impactful concepts at the
top.

# Pattern classification

Every concept-unit series is assigned a `pattern_type` label based on
which of ten rules match. When multiple rules match (the common case),
all matching labels are also stored in `pattern_tags`, and the primary
`pattern_type` is picked by precedence — favoring labels that specify
the *kind* of shift (which determines chart choice) over labels that
specify the *timing* alone.

## The ten pattern types

| `pattern_type` | Detection rule (features from the summary) |
| --- | --- |
| `stable` | `max_psi < 0.1` AND `n_regimes ≤ 1`. Short-circuits everything else |
| `bimodal_change` | `dip_pvalue_origin` and `dip_pvalue_current` disagree at α = 0.05 (unimodal ↔ bimodal) |
| `seasonal` | `seasonality_significant = TRUE` (|ACF@12| > 2/√n) |
| `transient_anomalies` | `n_regimes ≥ 2` AND `min_regime_length_months ≤ 2` AND `max_regime_length_months ≥ 6` |
| `scale_shift` | `n_regimes == 2` AND `\|delta_sd_pct\| > 20` AND `\|delta_mean_pct\| < 10` |
| `tail_shift` | `n_regimes == 2` AND (`\|delta_p5_pct\| > 15` OR `\|delta_p95_pct\| > 15`) AND `\|delta_mean_pct\| < 5` AND `\|delta_sd_pct\| < 15` |
| `location_shift` | `n_regimes == 2` AND `\|delta_mean_pct\| > 10` AND `\|delta_sd_pct\| < 20` |
| `monotonic_trend` | `trend_pvalue_mean < 0.05` AND `\|trend_tau_mean\| > 0.7` |
| `step_change` | `n_regimes == 2` AND both regime lengths ≥ 3 — fallback when no distributional pattern fires |
| `gradual_drift` | Fallback — drift exists but doesn't match any cleaner rule |

## Precedence for the primary label

1. `stable` (short-circuits — nothing else evaluated)
2. `bimodal_change`
3. `seasonal`
4. `transient_anomalies`
5. `scale_shift`
6. `tail_shift`
7. `location_shift`
8. `monotonic_trend`
9. `step_change`
10. `gradual_drift`

Distributional patterns (scale/tail/location/bimodal) win over temporal
patterns (trend/step) because they specify the *shape* of change and
therefore drive graph selection. If a concept has both a distributional
and a temporal pattern (very common — a step change usually shifts the
mean), the distributional label is primary and the temporal label goes
into `pattern_tags`.

## Recommended plots per pattern

The `pattern_type` maps directly to a suggested chart. A dashboard
implementation can use this to auto-select the drill-down view.

| `pattern_type` | Recommended primary plot | Recommended secondary plot | What to look for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `stable` | Sparkline of monthly mean | Sparkline of `n_obs` | No action expected — sanity check that data volume hasn't collapsed |
| `bimodal_change` | Ridgeline density plot, one row per year | Overlaid density: origin vs. current regime | The emergence (or disappearance) of a second mode. Often means two subpopulations mixed together, or a subcohort added/removed |
| `seasonal` | STL decomposition (`stats::stl`) of monthly mean | Monthly boxplot faceted by calendar month | Amplitude of the annual cycle; whether it's constant or growing/shrinking |
| `transient_anomalies` | Time series of monthly mean with anomaly months marked | Density plot of anomaly month(s) vs. surrounding regime | Investigate each transient month as a candidate ETL/ingest event; check surrounding calendar events |
| `scale_shift` | Violin or boxplot, one violin per regime | Time series of monthly SD | Cause is usually instrument recalibration, protocol change, or population change (e.g., adding pediatrics widens ranges) |
| `tail_shift` | Q-Q plot vs. origin baseline; or density plot with tails highlighted | Time series of p5 and p95 | Center stable, tails moving — often signals new extremes appearing (rare disease onset in cohort, sensor precision improvement) |
| `location_shift` | Violin per regime | Time series of monthly mean with regime bands shaded | Cause is typically unit change, coding change, or population case-mix shift |
| `monotonic_trend` | Line plot of monthly mean with linear/loess regression | Time series of `psi_origin` cumulative | Slow trends often reflect gradual population change (aging cohort) or cumulative measurement bias |
| `step_change` | Time series of monthly mean with regime bands shaded | Boxplot per regime | Rare as a primary — usually indicates a distributional signal that just didn't cross the thresholds |
| `gradual_drift` | Time series of monthly mean, SD, and `psi_origin` on a shared time axis | Density heatmap (from `_drift_histogram.csv`) | No clean pattern — inspect the raw metrics and look for slower/complex behavior |

## Cross-cutting suggestions

Regardless of the primary pattern, the following plots are always useful
during drill-down:

- **Time series of `psi_origin` and `psi_current`**, both on the same axis
  — shows whether drift is against the historical baseline, the current
  regime, or both.
- **Regime timeline bar** — a stacked horizontal bar with one segment per
  regime, sized by duration, colored by regime index. Instantly readable.
- **The three-CSV drill-down** — pair `_drift_monthly.csv` (a table of
  scores) with `_drift_histogram.csv` (heatmap-ready). Feeding the latter
  to `EHRtemporalVariability::estimateDataTemporalMap()` produces the
  IGT projection that is a de facto standard for OMOP data-drift visuals.

# Output files

Three CSVs are written alongside the existing `_stats.csv` and
`_value_as_concept_stats.csv` for every numeric concept check.

## `<baseFilePath>_drift_monthly.csv`

One row per (concept, unit, year_month). Primary artifact for
per-month drill-down.

| Column | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `measurement_concept_id` | Concept identifier |
| `unit_concept_id` | Unit concept (or `NA` for unit-less values) |
| `year_month` | Calendar month, `YYYY-MM` |
| `n_obs` | Non-NA value count for the month |
| `psi_origin` | PSI vs. origin baseline |
| `wasserstein_origin` | Wasserstein-1 vs. origin baseline, in value units |
| `jsd_origin` | Jensen-Shannon divergence (log2, in [0, 1]) vs. origin |
| `psi_current` | PSI vs. current regime baseline |
| `wasserstein_current` | Wasserstein-1 vs. current regime baseline |
| `jsd_current` | JSD vs. current regime baseline |
| `bcp_posterior` | Bayesian posterior that a change occurred *between* this month and the next (last month is always NA) |
| `regime_id` | Sequential regime identifier |
| `regime_length_months` | Total eligible months in this month's regime |
| `is_regime_start` | TRUE if this month is the first eligible month of a new regime |
| `is_anomaly` | TRUE if `psi_current > threshold` and not a regime start |
| `insufficient_data` | TRUE if `n_obs < minMonthObs` (drift metrics NA) |

## `<baseFilePath>_drift_summary.csv`

One row per (concept, unit). Dashboard sorting / triage artifact.

| Column | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `origin_baseline_start` / `origin_baseline_end` | Bounds of the fixed origin baseline window |
| `origin_n_months`, `origin_n_obs` | Origin baseline sample size |
| `n_bins` | Actual bin count (may be < 10 if origin values had ties) |
| `n_regimes` | Number of regimes detected across the whole series |
| `regime_change_months` | Semicolon-separated list of regime start months |
| `regime_lengths_months` | Semicolon-separated list of regime durations aligned with `regime_change_months` |
| `min_regime_length_months`, `max_regime_length_months` | Shortest and longest regime — used by the pattern classifier to distinguish transient blips from persistent shifts |
| `current_regime_start`, `current_regime_length_months` | The regime the latest month belongs to |
| `n_anomalous_months`, `anomalous_months` | Months flagged as within-regime anomalies |
| `max_psi_origin`, `max_psi_current`, `max_wasserstein_origin`, `max_wasserstein_current` | Peak drift scores across the series |
| `delta_mean_pct`, `delta_sd_pct`, `delta_p5_pct`, `delta_p95_pct` | Percent change in the value distribution's mean / SD / 5th / 95th percentile between the first and last regime. Drives location vs. scale vs. tail-shift classification |
| `trend_tau_mean`, `trend_pvalue_mean` | Mann-Kendall test on the monthly mean series — detects monotonic drift in central tendency. `tau` in [−1, 1] |
| `trend_tau_psi`, `trend_pvalue_psi` | Mann-Kendall test on the monthly `psi_origin` series — detects drift *accumulation* over time |
| `seasonality_acf_lag12`, `seasonality_significant` | Autocorrelation at lag 12 of the monthly mean series; TRUE if it exceeds the 95% white-noise threshold |
| `dip_stat_origin`, `dip_pvalue_origin`, `dip_stat_current`, `dip_pvalue_current` | Hartigan's dip test for unimodality on the origin and current-regime pooled distributions. p < 0.05 rejects unimodality |
| `priority_score` | `max(psi_origin, psi_current) * log10(1 + total_n_obs)` — sortable score combining drift magnitude and data volume. High priority = drifting concept with high traffic |
| `pattern_type` | Rule-based primary drift pattern label — see the Pattern Classification section |
| `pattern_tags` | Semicolon-separated list of all rules that matched. Useful when a concept has multiple simultaneous patterns |

## `<baseFilePath>_drift_histogram.csv`

One row per (concept, unit, year_month, bin). Reshape-ready for external
visualization tools (e.g., `EHRtemporalVariability::estimateDataTemporalMap()`).

| Column | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `bin_index` | Sequential bin id (1..n_bins) |
| `bin_lower`, `bin_upper` | Bin edges. First bin's lower is `-Inf`; last bin's upper is `+Inf` |
| `count` | Observation count in this bin for this month |
| `proportion` | Bin proportion (sums to 1 within month) |

# Interpreting results

## Reading each metric

| Metric | Range | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`psi_origin` / `psi_current`** | 0 to ~ (unbounded) | < 0.1 stable · 0.1–0.25 moderate drift · > 0.25 significant drift · > 1.0 severe (distributions barely overlap in binning). Origin comparison answers "how different from history?"; current answers "how different from recent normal?" |
| **`wasserstein_origin` / `wasserstein_current`** | 0 to ~ (in value units) | Interpreted directly in the measurement's units. E.g., Wasserstein of 3.2 for glucose in mg/dL means the current distribution's "mass" is shifted 3.2 mg/dL on average from the baseline. Compare against the clinical resolution of the measurement |
| **`jsd_origin` / `jsd_current`** | [0, 1] (log2) | 0 identical · < 0.05 minor · 0.05–0.15 moderate · > 0.15 major shape divergence. Bounded and symmetric — good for cross-concept comparison since scale doesn't depend on the measurement's units |
| **`bcp_posterior`** | [0, 1] | Probability that a regime change occurred *between* this month and the next. Above `bcpThreshold` (default 0.5) starts a new regime one month later. Values near 0.5 are uncertain — inspect visually |
| **`regime_length_months`** | 1 to N | 1–2: transient blip · 3–5: brief instability · 6+: persistent regime |
| **`trend_tau_mean`** | [−1, 1] | > 0 increasing · < 0 decreasing · magnitude reflects strength. Values around ±0.5 indicate a step-like change; values > ±0.7 with low p-value indicate a smooth trend |
| **`trend_tau_psi`** | [−1, 1] | Positive tau means drift is *accumulating* — each month is further from the origin baseline than the last. Watch this metric even when the mean is stable, as it can reveal slow shape change |
| **`seasonality_acf_lag12`** | [−1, 1] | > 0.3 typically indicates a real yearly cycle. Negative values mean anti-seasonality (this month tends to be opposite the same month a year ago — rare, usually a data problem) |
| **`dip_pvalue_origin` / `dip_pvalue_current`** | (0, 1] | < 0.05 rejects unimodality (distribution has ≥ 2 modes). Pattern classifier fires on a flip in significance between origin and current |
| **`delta_mean_pct`** | percent | First regime → last regime percent change in mean. > 10% typically actionable |
| **`delta_sd_pct`** | percent | Percent change in SD. > 20% typically actionable (usually reflects instrument or population change) |
| **`delta_p5_pct` / `delta_p95_pct`** | percent | Tail movement; > 15% with stable center signals new extremes appearing |
| **`priority_score`** | 0 to ~ | Higher = more urgent. Combines magnitude and volume. Sort dashboard descending by this |

## Regime durations tell you the story shape

The pattern of `regime_lengths_months` values indicates what happened:

- `[36]` — completely stable series, no drift
- `[18, 24]` — one persistent baseline shift after 18 months
- `[15, 1, 20]` — 1-month transient anomaly, followed by return to normal, then persistent shift
- `[10, 2, 4, 20]` — brief instability period, then stable new baseline

For actionable triage, filter regimes to those `regime_length_months >= 3`
to focus on persistent shifts, and inspect short (1–2 month) regimes
separately as candidate ETL / ingest anomalies.

## Origin vs. current comparisons answer different questions

- **`psi_origin` high, `psi_current` low** — the data has drifted from
  its historical baseline, but has been stable *recently*. The current
  regime is the "new normal."
- **`psi_origin` low, `psi_current` high** — recent months look different
  from the rest of their regime. Something is starting to happen; may
  precede a regime break in subsequent months.
- **Both high** — active, ongoing drift.

## Threshold calibration

Defaults (`driftPsiThreshold = 0.25`, `bcpThreshold = 0.5`) are calibrated
for concepts with several hundred observations per month and 10 bins.
Within a stable regime with this sample size, mean `psi_current` typically
sits around 0.05. Anything above 0.25 is a strong signal of month-vs-regime
divergence.

For lower-volume concepts (e.g., 30–100 obs/month), sampling noise inflates
PSI, and the 0.25 threshold may generate false positives. Consider raising
`driftPsiThreshold` or `minMonthObs`.

# Workup workflow

A pragmatic drill-down sequence for a flagged concept:

1. **Sort the drift summary by `priority_score` descending.** Investigate
   the top concepts first — they combine high drift with high volume.
2. **Read `pattern_type` and `pattern_tags`** to understand the *kind* of
   drift. Use the Recommended Plots table to pick the appropriate chart.
3. **Check the temporal shape** via `regime_change_months` +
   `regime_lengths_months` — is this a single break, a series of blips,
   or ongoing gradual drift?
4. **Confirm severity** by looking at the raw metrics:
   - `max_psi_origin` for magnitude vs. baseline
   - `max_psi_current` for magnitude vs. recent regime
   - `wasserstein_*` for magnitude in the measurement's units
5. **Compare origin vs. current**: if `psi_origin` is high but
   `psi_current` is low, the shift already happened and stabilized —
   consider updating the baseline. If both are high, drift is ongoing.
6. **Drill down to the monthly view** via `_drift_monthly.csv` and pair
   with `_drift_histogram.csv` for a per-month distributional snapshot.
7. **Cross-check nearby concepts** — if multiple related concepts (e.g.,
   all labs from the same panel) drift simultaneously in the same month,
   the cause is almost certainly ETL / ingestion / vendor-side, not
   clinical.
8. **Document and act** — the anomaly and regime months are precise
   enough to line up against ETL logs, vendor change notices, or
   protocol updates. If the drift was expected (e.g., new site added),
   consider treating the current regime as the new baseline for
   downstream analyses.

# Known limitations

- **Ineligible months create implicit gaps.** `bcp` treats the sequence of
  eligible months as contiguous even if calendar months are missing
  between them. For sparse concepts, a gap of many months followed by
  new data may be modeled as continuous change rather than a discontinuity.
- **`bcp` is stochastic.** MCMC-based methods produce slightly different
  posteriors on each run. If exact reproducibility is required, wrap
  `executeDqChecks()` in a `set.seed()` call.
- **PSI is unbounded above** and can produce very large values (10+) for
  distributions with disjoint support. Cap for visualization purposes.
- **Drift is currently computed per (concept, unit) independently.** A
  unit switch (e.g., mg/dL → mmol/L) will appear as two separate groups,
  each with its own baseline — not as drift within a single group.

# References

- Barry, D., & Hartigan, J. A. (1993). A Bayesian analysis for change point problems. *JASA*, 88(421), 309–319.
- Erdman, C., & Emerson, J. W. (2007). bcp: An R package for performing a Bayesian analysis of change point problems. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 23(3).
- Sáez, C., Gutiérrez-Sacristán, A., Kohane, I., García-Gómez, J. M., & Avillach, P. (2020). EHRtemporalVariability: delineating temporal data-set shifts in electronic health records. *GigaScience*, 9(8), giaa079.
- Taplin, R., & Hunt, C. (2019). The population accuracy index: a new measure of population stability for model monitoring. *Risks*, 7(2), 53.
